chapter: Chapter 5: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
source: NCERT Class 8 Social Science (Exploring Society: India and Beyond — Part 1)

questions.question: What does the word 'franchise' (or 'suffrage') mean in a democracy?
options: The right to start a factory
questions.explanation: Franchise (also called suffrage) means the right to vote granted to citizens by the Constitution or government.

questions.question: Which word has the same meaning as 'franchise' in the NCERT Class 8 Civics chapter?
questions.explanation: Both 'franchise' and 'suffrage' mean the right to vote.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution gives the right to Universal Adult Franchise?
questions.explanation: Article 326 of the Indian Constitution provides that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies are based on universal adult suffrage.

questions.question: What is the minimum age to vote in elections in India?
questions.explanation: Every Indian citizen aged 18 years and above has the right to vote under Universal Adult Franchise.

questions.question: Before 1988, what was the minimum voting age in India?
questions.explanation: Earlier, the minimum voting age in India was 21 years; it was lowered to 18 years in 1988.

questions.question: In which year did India lower the voting age from 21 years to 18 years?
questions.explanation: India lowered the minimum voting age from 21 to 18 in 1988, giving millions of young citizens the right to vote.

questions.question: Who said in the Constituent Assembly in November 1949 that India adopted adult franchise with 'abundant faith in the common man'?
questions.explanation: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar made this famous remark in the Constituent Assembly Debates in November 1949.

questions.question: What does 'one person, one vote, one value' mean?
options: Every adult citizen gets one vote and every vote has equal value
One person can vote for their whole family
Only educated people get one vote
questions.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise guarantees that every adult citizen has one vote, all votes carry equal value, and nobody can vote on someone else's behalf.

questions.question: Can a family member legally go to a polling booth and vote on behalf of an elderly parent?
options: Yes, with a letter from the parent
No, nobody can vote on another person's behalf
Yes, if they live in the same house
questions.explanation: Every citizen must cast their own vote; no one is allowed to vote on another person's behalf.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect an Indian citizen's right to vote?
options: Having their name on the voter list
Caste, religion, gender, wealth, or education
questions.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise gives voting rights to all adult citizens regardless of caste, creed, religion, gender, wealth, or education.

questions.question: In which case can an adult Indian citizen be legally stopped from voting?
options: If they live in a village
If found guilty of certain serious crimes
If they do not own land or a house
If they have not finished school
questions.explanation: An adult Indian citizen can be barred from voting only if convicted of certain serious crimes.

questions.question: About what percentage of Indians had the right to vote before Independence?
questions.explanation: Before Independence, voting was not universal and only about 13% of Indians were allowed to vote.

questions.question: In 1947, India's overall literacy rate was about:
questions.explanation: In 1947, India's overall literacy rate was about 14% (and only about 8% among women).

questions.question: In 1947, what was the approximate literacy rate among women in India?
questions.explanation: In 1947, literacy among women was only about 8%, yet India boldly granted equal voting rights to women right from the start.

questions.question: Why did India adopt Universal Adult Franchise right after Independence even though literacy was low?
options: There were very few people in India
Foreign countries forced India to do so
Only literate people were allowed to vote in villages
Constitution makers believed every adult citizen is equal and capable of choosing leaders
questions.explanation: India's Constitution makers had full faith in the common people and believed democracy must treat all adult citizens equally.

questions.question: In which year did women in Switzerland finally get the right to vote?
questions.explanation: Unlike India, which gave women voting rights from the beginning, Switzerland granted voting rights to women only in 1971.

questions.question: Figure 5.3 in the NCERT chapter shows a historic Women's Suffrage Parade held in which country and year?
questions.explanation: Figure 5.3 depicts the 1913 Women's Suffrage Parade in the USA, showing the long struggle women faced for voting rights in many nations.

questions.question: About how many elected representatives serve across India's 250,000+ local government bodies?
questions.explanation: India has about 3.1 million elected representatives across more than 250,000 local government bodies.

questions.question: Out of the 3.1 million elected representatives in India's local government bodies, about how many are women?
questions.explanation: Around 1.3 million out of the 3.1 million local body representatives in India are women.

questions.question: What is a 'constituency'?
options: A machine used to count votes
A fixed area whose voters elect one representative to a legislative body
A list of rules made by a school
questions.explanation: A constituency is a geographical area whose registered voters elect a representative to a body like the Lok Sabha or State Assembly.

questions.question: How does the NCERT textbook define a 'system'?
options: A single law passed by the President
A group of connected parts working together for a common purpose
questions.explanation: A system is a group of interconnected or interdependent elements working together for a common purpose.

questions.question: How does Universal Adult Franchise keep elected leaders answerable to the people?
options: Voters can vote them out in the next election if they do not work well
questions.explanation: Because every adult citizen holds a vote, elected representatives remain accountable to the people and can be replaced in the next election.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of Universal Adult Franchise shown in Fig. 5.4?
options: Keeping only one political party in power forever
questions.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise promotes equality, accountability, and civic participation—never one-party rule.

questions.question: Who is eligible to vote in India's general elections?
options: Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above who is registered on the voter list
Only citizens who pay income tax
Only citizens living in big cities
Only citizens who have a college degree
questions.explanation: Any Indian citizen aged 18 years or above whose name is on the electoral roll can vote.

questions.question: When did India grant women the right to vote?
options: Right from the beginning of our Constitution after Independence
questions.explanation: India was among the early nations to give women equal voting rights from the very start of independent democratic governance.

questions.question: Universal Adult Franchise gives every adult citizen the power to:
options: Choose their own representatives and shape the country's future
questions.explanation: By voting, every adult citizen helps decide who governs and plays a role in shaping the nation's future.

questions.question: Approximately how many voters were eligible to vote in India's 2024 Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: In the 2024 Lok Sabha General Elections, over 968 million Indian citizens were eligible to vote.

questions.question: Roughly how many polling stations were set up across India during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: More than 1 million polling stations were set up across India for the 2024 general elections.

questions.question: According to the NCERT textbook, India's eligible voter population is about how many times the population of the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: India's eligible voter population is around 15 times the total population of the United Kingdom.

questions.question: In land area, India is approximately how many times larger than France?
questions.explanation: India's geographical area is about 6 times larger than France.

questions.question: Why does the textbook compare India with the UK and France on Page 121?
options: To prove India copies their voting machines
To show the huge scale and geographical diversity of Indian elections
To show that France has more voters than India
To explain why India does not need polling booths
questions.explanation: The comparison helps students understand how massive and complex conducting elections in India is.

questions.question: Which new accessibility facility was introduced for the first time in the 2024 General Elections?
options: Home voting for the elderly and persons with disabilities
questions.explanation: For the first time in 2024, senior citizens (elderly) and persons with disabilities could cast their votes from home.

questions.question: Which facilities does the ECI provide for visually impaired and mobility-challenged voters?
options: Separate voting only in big cities
Braille voter cards, ramps, wheelchairs, and app-based help
questions.explanation: The ECI provides Braille-enabled voter cards, ramps, wheelchairs, and app-based assistance so every citizen can vote comfortably.

questions.question: How can persons with disabilities request wheelchairs or assistance at a polling booth?
options: By writing to the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The ECI provides app-based requests for assistance such as wheelchairs and volunteers at polling stations.

questions.question: Which voting method helps certain eligible voters (such as those on election duty or essential services) who cannot visit their polling booth?
questions.explanation: Postal voting (postal ballots) allows specific categories of eligible voters to cast their votes even when they cannot reach the booth.

questions.question: What remarkable step has India's election machinery taken in remote areas to make sure 'no voter is left behind'?
options: Letting the village head vote for everyone
Setting up a polling station even for a single voter
Asking remote villagers to travel to Delhi
questions.explanation: Election officials travel to remote locations and have even set up a polling booth for a single eligible woman voter.

questions.question: About what percentage of eligible voters did NOT vote in the 2024 General Elections?
questions.explanation: Roughly 34% of eligible voters did not cast their votes in the 2024 elections.

questions.question: If about 34% of eligible voters did not vote in 2024, about what percentage DID vote?
questions.explanation: 100% minus 34% gives approximately 66% voter participation in the 2024 elections.

questions.question: The Uttaramerur inscriptions (in Tamil Nadu), which describe an ancient Indian way of selecting representatives, belong to which century?
questions.explanation: The 10th-century Uttaramerur inscriptions record a fair and transparent method of choosing local representatives.

questions.question: In the Uttaramerur selection method, what were the names of eligible candidates written on?
questions.explanation: Candidates' names were written on fragments of palm leaves and placed inside a sealed pot.

questions.question: In the Uttaramerur process, who drew the palm leaves randomly out of the sealed pot in public?
questions.explanation: A young boy drew the palm leaves randomly one by one in front of everyone so the selection stayed completely fair.

questions.question: In the Uttaramerur process, why did the respected reader show his empty hands to the public before reading the palm leaves?
options: To prove there was no cheating or hidden palm leaf
To signal the end of harvest
questions.explanation: Showing empty hands ensured complete transparency and fairness before the whole community.

questions.question: Who was the first voter in independent India's general elections of 1951?
questions.explanation: Shyam Saran Negi, a school teacher from Himachal Pradesh, was independent India's first voter in 1951.

questions.question: Shyam Saran Negi belonged to which state, and at what age did he cast his vote in 2017 (Fig. 5.15)?
questions.explanation: Shyam Saran Negi was a school teacher from Himachal Pradesh who voted even at the age of 100 in 2017.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School Grade 8 Class Representative election, who were the three candidates?
questions.explanation: Ahmed, Gurmat, and Ravi contested the Grade 8 Class Representative election at Suryodaya School.

questions.question: Who acted as the Election Officer for the Grade 8 election at Suryodaya School?
questions.explanation: Ms. Usha, the class teacher, served as the Election Officer to conduct the election fairly.

questions.question: What did Ahmed promise if elected in the Suryodaya School election?
questions.explanation: Ahmed promised to improve the cleanliness of the classrooms and playground, and campaigned using posters.

questions.question: What did Gurmat promise in the Suryodaya School election?
options: A system of peer coaching and mutual support to help classmates learn better
questions.explanation: Gurmat promised peer coaching and mutual support for learning, and campaigned via the noticeboard and talking to classmates.

questions.question: How did Ravi campaign for his promise of more music, theatre, and visual arts in the timetable?
options: By holding a lunchtime music performance
By writing on the noticeboard only
questions.explanation: Ravi held a lunchtime music performance to promote his plan for more arts in the timetable.

questions.question: Why did Ms. Usha prepare a special Braille ballot paper for the class election?
options: So Neha, a visually impaired student, could vote privately and independently
questions.explanation: The Braille ballot paper allowed Neha to cast a secret vote independently, just like ECI's inclusive measures.

questions.question: What mark were Suryodaya School students asked to put next to their chosen candidate's name?
questions.explanation: Students marked an 'X' next to the chosen candidate's name without writing their own name to keep the vote secret.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a 'secret ballot'?
options: To let teachers see everyone's vote
To keep every voter's choice private so they can vote without fear or pressure
questions.explanation: A secret ballot protects a voter's privacy so nobody can pressure or threaten them for their choice.

questions.question: How did Ms. Usha keep the ballot box safe until counting time?
options: She sealed the ballot box until counting began
She left it open on her desk
She counted each slip loudly during voting
She gave it to Ahmed to hold
questions.explanation: Sealing the ballot box prevents tampering and ensures fair counting.

questions.question: Why did Ms. Usha call Ms. Sheeba from the next class during vote counting?
options: To act as an independent witness so counting stays fair and transparent
questions.explanation: Having Ms. Sheeba watch the counting ensured fairness and transparency.

questions.question: Why was one ballot paper declared invalid in the Suryodaya School election?
questions.explanation: A ballot paper with no 'X' marked next to any candidate is invalid and cannot be counted.

questions.question: Gurmat won the class election with 12 votes out of 33 cast (Ahmed 8, Ravi 10). Which voting principle does this show?
options: First-Past-The-Post, where the candidate with the most votes wins even with less than 50%
questions.explanation: Even though 12 is less than half of 33, Gurmat won because she had the highest number of votes—this is First-Past-The-Post.

questions.question: How did Ahmed and Ravi behave after Gurmat won the class election?
options: They congratulated her and offered to support her
They refused to sit in class
They demanded a re-election every week
questions.explanation: Congratulating the winner and working together shows healthy democratic spirit.

questions.question: What is the full form of NOTA?
questions.explanation: NOTA stands for 'None Of The Above', letting voters reject all contesting candidates.

questions.question: What happens if many voters choose the NOTA option in an Indian election?
options: The seat stays empty for 5 years
All candidates are sent to jail
It does not change the result, but sends a strong message that voters want better candidates
questions.explanation: NOTA does not alter who wins, but it acts as a quiet yet powerful message that voters are unhappy with the choices.

questions.question: If a school council is elected ONLY by the Class Representatives (and not by all students), what type of election is it?
questions.explanation: When elected representatives vote to choose a higher body, it is an indirect election (just like Rajya Sabha elections).

questions.question: What type of institution is the Election Commission of India (ECI)?
options: A department under the Prime Minister
A committee of the Lok Sabha Speaker
questions.explanation: The ECI is an independent constitutional body that conducts free and fair elections in India.

questions.question: In which year was the Election Commission of India (ECI) established?
questions.explanation: The Election Commission of India was set up in 1950.

questions.question: In which years were independent India's first general elections held?
questions.explanation: Independent India's first general elections were held in 1951–1952.

questions.question: Where is the headquarters (main office) of the Election Commission of India located?
questions.explanation: The main office of the Election Commission of India is in Delhi.

questions.question: Why must the Election Commission of India be independent?
options: So it can appoint Chief Ministers
So it can pass laws instead of Parliament
So it can hold free and fair elections without pressure from any government or party
So it can favour the ruling party
questions.explanation: Independence ensures the ECI applies election rules equally and fairly to every party, including the party in power.

questions.question: Which elections are conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI)?
options: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Assemblies, President, and Vice President
Only Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The ECI oversees elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, President, and Vice President.

questions.question: Which elections are NOT conducted directly by the Election Commission of India?
options: Gram Panchayat and Urban Local Body elections
questions.explanation: Gram Panchayat and Urban Local Body elections are managed by State Election Commissions.

questions.question: Which body manages direct elections to Gram Panchayats and Urban Local Bodies?
questions.explanation: State Election Commissions conduct grassroots local body elections in consultation with the ECI.

questions.question: At the national level, the Election Commission of India consists of:
options: One Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners
One Chief Election Commissioner and five Election Commissioners
questions.explanation: At the national level, the ECI has one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and two Election Commissioners.

questions.question: Who heads the election machinery at the State or Union Territory level?
questions.explanation: At the State/UT level, the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) oversees election work.

questions.question: Who oversees election management at the District level?
questions.explanation: The District Election Officer (DEO) manages election work at the district level.

questions.question: What is the main duty of a Returning Officer (RO)?
questions.explanation: According to Fig. 5.11, the Returning Officer (RO) conducts elections in a constituency.

questions.question: Which official is responsible for managing and updating the voter list (electoral roll)?
questions.explanation: The Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) manages the voter list.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key function of the Election Commission of India (Fig. 5.9)?
options: Setting election dates and registering political parties
questions.explanation: The ECI sets election dates, registers political parties, enforces the Model Code of Conduct, and oversees the whole election process.

questions.question: Which of these tasks is also performed by the ECI during elections?
options: Enforcing the Model Code of Conduct
questions.explanation: Enforcing the Model Code of Conduct is one of the four core duties of the ECI shown in Fig. 5.9.

questions.question: Who are commonly deployed across India to help conduct polling at over 1 million booths?
questions.explanation: Large numbers of government staff, including school teachers, are deployed on election duty across India.

questions.question: Which level of ECI official works directly below the National level (Chief Election Commissioner)?
questions.explanation: The ECI hierarchy flows from National level (CEC & 2 ECs) → State/UT level (CEO) → District level (DEO) → RO & ERO.

questions.question: Under whom do the Returning Officer (RO) and Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) work?
questions.explanation: Fig. 5.11 shows the RO and ERO functioning at the district/constituency level under the District Election Officer.

questions.question: In India's parliamentary democracy, citizens directly elect MPs to the Lok Sabha and MLAs to the:
options: State and Union Territory Legislative Assemblies
questions.explanation: Citizens directly vote to elect MPs to the Lok Sabha and MLAs to State/UT Legislative Assemblies.

questions.question: What is the full form of EVM?
questions.explanation: EVM stands for Electronic Voting Machine.

questions.question: What is the full form of VVPAT?
questions.explanation: VVPAT stands for Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail.

questions.question: Which official card is issued by the ECI as proof of voter registration?
questions.explanation: The Voter ID Card (Electors Photo Identity Card / EPIC) proves a citizen is registered to vote.

questions.question: Can a citizen vote if their name is NOT on the voter list (electoral roll)?
options: Yes, by showing any school ID
Yes, if a candidate signs a paper
No, being registered on the voter list is mandatory
Yes, only in Lok Sabha elections
questions.explanation: An eligible citizen must be registered on their constituency's electoral roll in order to vote.

questions.question: Inside a polling booth, what does the 1st Polling Officer do?
options: Puts ink on the voter's finger
Checks the voter's name on the voter list and verifies ID proof
questions.explanation: The 1st Polling Officer checks the voter's name on the voter list and verifies their ID.

questions.question: What does the 2nd Polling Officer do inside a polling booth?
options: Checks the voter's name on the voter list
Collects the chit and activates the EVM
Inks the voter's finger, gives a chit, and takes the voter's signature
questions.explanation: The 2nd Polling Officer applies indelible ink, issues a voter chit, and takes the voter's signature.

questions.question: What does the 3rd Polling Officer do before the voter goes to the EVM?
options: Puts ink on the voter's finger
Takes the voter chit and checks the inked finger
Hands over the VVPAT slip to take home
questions.explanation: The 3rd Polling Officer collects the chit, checks the inked finger, and enables the EVM for voting.

questions.question: Why is indelible (hard-to-wash) ink put on a voter's finger?
options: To stop anyone from voting more than once in the same election
To show which party the voter chose
questions.explanation: Indelible ink marks that a person has already voted, preventing duplicate or fake voting.

questions.question: Which sound confirms that your vote has been recorded after pressing the button on an EVM?
options: A bell rung by an officer
questions.explanation: A beep sound confirms the vote is recorded, and the VVPAT displays the printed slip.

questions.question: How does a voter check that their vote went to the right candidate on the EVM?
options: By taking a paper receipt home
By getting an SMS on their phone
By seeing the printed paper slip inside the VVPAT window
questions.explanation: The VVPAT machine prints a paper slip visible through a glass window so the voter can verify their choice.

questions.question: Can a voter take the VVPAT printed slip home?
options: No, it drops into a sealed box inside the VVPAT machine to keep voting secret
Only elderly voters can take it home
questions.explanation: The VVPAT slip stays inside a sealed compartment so the vote remains secret and serves as an audit backup.

questions.question: Why is the VVPAT paper trail useful during elections?
options: It connects EVMs to the internet
It lets voters change their vote the next day
It lets voters verify their vote and provides a physical paper backup for recounting if needed
questions.explanation: VVPAT builds trust by showing the voter their choice and keeping a physical paper record for verification or recounting.

questions.question: Where is the NOTA button found during Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections?
options: On the EVM ballot unit along with the candidates' buttons
questions.explanation: NOTA is provided as a button right on the EVM ballot unit.

questions.question: Which of these is a major advantage of EVMs over paper ballots?
options: Faster counting, higher accuracy, and less paper waste (eco-friendly)
Removing the need for polling stations
Cutting down more trees for paper
Showing everyone who voted for whom
questions.explanation: EVMs save paper, prevent smudged/invalid marks, and make counting faster and more accurate.

questions.question: Which two countries mentioned in the NCERT textbook have used India's EVM and VVPAT systems with ECI support?
questions.explanation: Namibia and Bhutan have used India's EVMs and VVPATs with support from the Election Commission of India.

questions.question: How has the ECI helped other countries interested in electronic voting?
options: By supporting countries like Namibia and Bhutan and offering training
By sending only paper ballot boxes
By keeping EVMs completely secret from all countries
questions.explanation: India's ECI has supported Namibia and Bhutan and trained several other countries interested in adopting EVMs and VVPATs.

questions.question: Which polling officer takes the voter's signature after putting ink on their finger?
questions.explanation: The 2nd Polling Officer applies ink, hands over the chit, and takes the voter's signature.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step a voter completes upon entering an Indian polling station?
options: Getting their name checked on the voter list and ID verified by the 1st Polling Officer
Pressing the button on the EVM
Submitting the chit to the 3rd Polling Officer
questions.explanation: The voting sequence starts with the 1st Polling Officer checking the voter's name on the electoral roll and verifying ID proof.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: What is the Model Code of Conduct (MCC)?
options: A set of dos and don'ts for political parties, leaders, and candidates to ensure free and fair elections
A guide for counting votes in Parliament
questions.explanation: The MCC lists rules of conduct that political parties and candidates must follow so elections remain peaceful, free, and fair.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: In which state and year was the Model Code of Conduct first voluntarily adopted?
questions.explanation: Major political parties in Kerala first voluntarily adopted the Model Code of Conduct in 1960.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: During which general elections did the ECI first share the Model Code of Conduct with political parties?
questions.explanation: After Kerala's 1960 step, the ECI circulated the MCC to political parties during the 1962 general elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: From which year did the ECI become proactive in strictly enforcing the Model Code of Conduct?
questions.explanation: From 1991 onwards, the ECI began proactively and strictly enforcing the Model Code of Conduct.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Who enforces the Model Code of Conduct during Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections?
questions.explanation: The ECI enforces the Model Code of Conduct and acts on complaints of violations.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Why is the ruling party NOT allowed to announce new government schemes after election dates are declared?
options: To save money for foreign trips
So it cannot misuse government resources to unfairly influence voters
questions.explanation: The MCC ensures a fair contest by stopping the ruling party from announcing new schemes or using official resources to sway voters.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: If a Chief Minister announces a new free laptop scheme two days after election dates are declared, it is:
options: A violation of the Model Code of Conduct
Allowed because they are Chief Minister
questions.explanation: Once the MCC is in force, no new government schemes or projects can be announced to influence voters.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: A candidate distributes sarees and household appliances to voters before polling day (Fig. 5.17). This violates:
questions.explanation: Giving gifts like sarees, appliances, or money to influence voters is strictly banned under the MCC.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Bundles of ₹500 notes are found in a candidate's car during election checks (Fig. 5.20). What does this show?
options: Illegal use of money power to bribe voters, violating the MCC
questions.explanation: Carrying unaccounted cash to distribute to voters violates the MCC and shows the challenge of money power.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Why are government officials NOT allowed to campaign for the ruling party (Fig. 5.19)?
options: Government officials must stay neutral during elections
questions.explanation: Government machinery and officials must remain impartial and cannot be used to help any political party.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Using abusive language against a rival candidate during speeches (Fig. 5.18) goes against the MCC rule of:
options: Keeping elections peaceful, respectful, and disciplined
questions.explanation: Candidates must show restraint and avoid abusive language so elections stay peaceful.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which of the following IS allowed during election campaigning under the MCC?
options: Peacefully sharing a party's manifesto and plans with voters
Using government cars for party rallies
questions.explanation: Parties and candidates can peacefully explain their promises and policies without bribing or misusing government resources.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: In which year did T.N. Seshan become the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan became Chief Election Commissioner in 1990 and brought major reforms to ensure free and fair elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which reform did T.N. Seshan introduce to stop proxy voting (fake voting in someone else's name)?
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan introduced Voter ID cards specifically to eliminate proxy voting.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Besides Voter ID cards, what other reforms did T.N. Seshan bring?
options: Strict campaigning rules and close watch on candidate spending
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan enforced precise campaigning rules, introduced Voter IDs, and kept strict vigilance on candidate spending.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Why is T.N. Seshan famously remembered in India?
options: He was India's first voter in 1951
He made Indian elections fairer, more transparent, and fearless
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan worked tirelessly to protect voters' rights and is remembered for making Indian elections fairer, transparent, and fearless.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What joyful phrase is often used to describe elections in India?
questions.explanation: Elections in India are fondly called the 'Festival of Democracy'.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Into how many constituencies is India divided for Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: India is divided into 543 parliamentary constituencies for Lok Sabha elections.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Out of 543 Lok Sabha seats, how many are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST)?
questions.explanation: In the 543-seat Lok Sabha, 84 seats are reserved for SCs, 47 for STs, and 412 are General seats.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How many General (unreserved) seats are there in the 543-member Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation: 543 total seats minus 84 SC and 47 ST reserved seats equals 412 General seats.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Why are some seats in the Lok Sabha reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST)?
options: To ensure fair representation for historically marginalised communities in Parliament
To make the Lok Sabha term longer
To reduce the total number of constituencies
Because SCs and STs cannot vote in General seats
questions.explanation: Reserved constituencies ensure that historically disadvantaged communities have fair representation in Parliament.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which voting system is used for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections?
questions.explanation: Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections use the First-Past-The-Post system, where the candidate with the most votes wins.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which House of Parliament is directly elected by citizens and called the 'Lower House'?
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha is the Lower House of Parliament, directly elected by voters to deal with national issues.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the main difference between an MP and an MLA?
options: MPs are nominated while MLAs are elected
MPs represent people in the national Parliament; MLAs represent people in the State Assembly
Only MPs are elected by citizens
MLAs work on foreign policy; MPs run village panchayats
questions.explanation: Members of Parliament (MPs) focus on national issues in Parliament, while Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs) focus on state/regional issues.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What are two regional names for the State Legislative Assembly mentioned in NCERT?
questions.explanation: The State Legislative Assembly is known regionally by names such as Vidhan Sabha and Niyama Sabha.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How is a Lok Sabha constituency related in size to State Assembly constituencies?
options: One Lok Sabha constituency usually contains two or more State Assembly constituencies
Lok Sabha constituencies exist only in Delhi
One State Assembly constituency contains 5 Lok Sabha constituencies
They are always the exact same size
questions.explanation: A single Lok Sabha (parliamentary) constituency is larger and typically includes two or more State Assembly constituencies.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is a 'coalition'?
options: One party winning all seats alone
Two or more political parties joining together to form a majority
Merging Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: When no single party wins a majority, two or more parties form a coalition to work together and form the government.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Who normally becomes the Prime Minister of India?
options: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha
The Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha typically becomes the Prime Minister.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Who normally becomes the Chief Minister of a state?
options: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the State Legislative Assembly
The Chief Electoral Officer of the state
questions.explanation: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the State Legislative Assembly becomes the Chief Minister.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the other constitutional name of the Rajya Sabha (Fig. 5.23)?
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha (Upper House) is also called the Council of States.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How many total members does the Rajya Sabha have?
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha has 245 members in total: 233 elected by MLAs and 12 nominated by the President.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How are the 245 members of the Rajya Sabha chosen?
options: 233 are indirectly elected by State/UT MLAs, and 12 are nominated by the President
All 245 are directly elected by citizens
200 are elected by MPs and 45 by Governors
All 245 are nominated by the Prime Minister
questions.explanation: 233 Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected by MLAs, and 12 distinguished citizens are nominated by the President.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India?
questions.explanation: The President of India nominates 12 distinguished persons to the Rajya Sabha.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Why is the Rajya Sabha called a 'Permanent House'?
options: It meets every single day of the year
Its building is older than the Lok Sabha
Its members stay for their whole life
It is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved—instead, one-third of its members retire every two years and new ones are elected.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the term of each member of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.explanation: Each Rajya Sabha member serves a 6-year term.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What fraction of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years?
questions.explanation: One-third (1/3) of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years, keeping the House continuous.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: On what basis are Rajya Sabha seats given to different states?
options: Population of the state (e.g., Uttar Pradesh has more seats than Arunachal Pradesh)
Number of rivers in the state
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha seats are allotted based on state population, so more populous states like Uttar Pradesh have more seats than Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which voting system is used in Rajya Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: MLAs elect Rajya Sabha members using the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system, ranking candidates in order of preference.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What does 'dissolution' mean for a legislative house like the Lok Sabha?
options: Suspending one member for a day
Ending of the house when its term finishes or for another Constitutional reason
questions.explanation: Dissolution means the expiry or termination of a legislative house due to the end of its term or another Constitutional reason.

questions.question: How is the President of India elected?
questions.explanation: The President of India is elected indirectly by an Electoral College.

questions.question: Who votes in the Electoral College that elects the President of India?
options: All nominated and elected MPs and MLCs
Elected MPs of Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha + Elected MLAs of all States and Delhi & Puducherry
Only Chief Ministers of all states
questions.explanation: The President's Electoral College includes elected MPs of both Houses of Parliament and elected MLAs of all States plus Delhi and Puducherry.

questions.question: Which two Union Territories' elected MLAs vote in the election of the President of India (as named in NCERT)?
options: Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli
questions.explanation: The NCERT chapter specifically mentions that elected MLAs of the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry vote in the Presidential election.

questions.question: Why does the President's Electoral College include both Union MPs and State/UT MLAs?
options: To make it faster than First-Past-The-Post
Because the President represents the whole country, combining support of both central and state legislatures
Because there are too few MPs in Delhi
Because MLAs cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections
questions.explanation: Including both elected MPs and elected MLAs ensures the President represents both the Union and the States.

questions.question: Who is NOT allowed to vote in the election of the President of India?
options: Elected MPs of the Lok Sabha
Elected MPs of the Rajya Sabha
Nominated MPs/MLAs and Members of State Legislative Councils (MLCs)
Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry
questions.explanation: Nominated members of Parliament/Assemblies and all Members of State Legislative Councils (MLCs) cannot vote in the Presidential election.

questions.question: Why are nominated members NOT allowed to vote in the election of the President?
options: So that only elected representatives choose the President
Because they do not attend Parliament
Because they are not Indian citizens
questions.explanation: Excluding nominated members ensures the President is elected solely by people's elected representatives.

questions.question: What is a 'bicameral legislature'?
options: A legislature that meets twice a year
A legislature with two separate houses or chambers
A legislature elected every two years
A legislature with only two political parties
questions.explanation: A bicameral legislature has two chambers/houses (such as Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, or Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council).

questions.question: In states that have both a Legislative Assembly (MLAs) and a Legislative Council (MLCs), who votes for the President?
options: Only elected MLAs (MLCs do not vote)
questions.explanation: Members of Legislative Councils (MLCs) are excluded from the President's Electoral College; only elected MLAs vote.

questions.question: In the Presidential election, why do states with larger populations have a greater say?
options: Because big states nominate 12 MPs each
Because voting rules give more weight to states with larger populations
Because smaller states are not allowed to vote
questions.explanation: The Presidential election uses special vote-counting rules so more populous states have a proportionally bigger say.

questions.question: Who elects the Vice President of India?
options: Both elected and nominated MPs of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The Vice President is elected by both elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament.

questions.question: Do State MLAs vote in the election of the Vice President of India?
options: No, only MPs of both Houses of Parliament vote
Only MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry vote
questions.explanation: State MLAs vote for the President, but NOT for the Vice President.

questions.question: Can the 12 nominated members of the Rajya Sabha vote in the Vice President's election?
options: Only if the Prime Minister allows
Yes, both elected and nominated MPs vote for the Vice President
Only when there is a tie
No, nominated members never vote in any election
questions.explanation: Unlike the Presidential election, the Vice President's Electoral College includes both elected and nominated MPs of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: Who is the Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha?
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: The Vice President of India serves as the Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: Who steps in to perform the President's duties if the President is unable to discharge them?
questions.explanation: If the President is unable to perform their functions, the Vice President steps in.

questions.question: Which voting system is shared by ALL THREE indirect elections—Rajya Sabha, President, and Vice President?
options: Direct secret ballot by all citizens
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha MPs, the President, and the Vice President are all elected indirectly through the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system.

questions.question: Which pair correctly separates DIRECT elections from INDIRECT elections in India?
options: Direct: Vice President | Indirect: Gram Panchayat
Direct: Rajya Sabha | Indirect: State Assembly
Direct: Lok Sabha & State Assembly | Indirect: Rajya Sabha, President & Vice President
questions.explanation: Citizens directly elect Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, and local bodies; Rajya Sabha, President, and Vice President are elected indirectly.

questions.question: Which three major challenges to Indian elections are highlighted in the NCERT chapter?
options: Too few voters, lack of languages, and too many holidays
Lack of paper, short terms, and too few parties
Money power, candidates with criminal records, and voter apathy (especially in urban areas)
No EVMs, no polling booths, and ban on campaigning
questions.explanation: The textbook lists growing influence of money, candidates with criminal records, and voter apathy (especially in cities) as major challenges.

questions.question: Where is 'voter apathy' (people not coming out to vote) noted as a special concern in India?
questions.explanation: The NCERT chapter highlights low voter turnout and voter apathy particularly in urban areas.

questions.question: What does 'voter apathy' mean?
options: Voting twice in the same election
Lack of interest or unwillingness among citizens to go out and vote
Standing as a candidate in two seats
questions.explanation: Voter apathy refers to citizens not taking interest in voting or skipping elections.

questions.question: What is a challenge of social media during elections mentioned in the chapter's activities?
options: It stops youth from hearing speeches
Catchy reels and fake/misleading information can confuse voters
questions.explanation: While social media spreads awareness, misleading content and catchy reels can confuse voters if they are not careful.

questions.question: Which three forces must work together to help voters—especially youth—make wise choices?
questions.explanation: Media, education, and awareness campaigns must work together to empower informed and responsible voters.

questions.question: According to the NCERT chapter, what is 'the strongest safeguard of a democratic system'?
questions.explanation: The textbook concludes that an aware and vigilant voter is the strongest safeguard of a democracy.

questions.question: Which website is suggested in the textbook's end-of-chapter activities to explore past Indian constituency election results?
questions.explanation: Question 9 of the chapter's activities invites students to explore constituency results on https://www.indiavotes.com.

questions.question: Complete the chapter's closing line: 'It starts with asking the right questions — and ends with...'
questions.explanation: The chapter closes with: 'It starts with asking the right questions — and ends with casting a responsible vote.'
